paragraphs.greek: Κατάλογος τρισχιλίων πολιτῶν ἦν. τοὺς μὲν ἐν τῷ καταλόγῳ ὄντας τὴν βουλὴν πρὸ τοῦ θανάτου κρίνειν ἔδει, τοὺς δὲ ἔξω οἱ Τριάκοντα ἀποκτείνειν ἐδύναντο. ὁ κατάλογος οὖν οὐκ ἦν τῶν ὀνομάτων γραφὴ μόνον, ἀλλὰ πρὸς τὴν ἀσφάλειαν διαφορὰν ἐποίει. ὁ Θηραμένης τῶν ἐν τῷ καταλόγῳ ἦν καὶ τὴν κρίσιν τῆς βουλῆς ἠξίου.

Ὁ Κριτίας, ὁρῶν τὴν βουλὴν εὐμενῶς πρὸς Θηραμένην ἔχουσαν, οὐκ ἐβούλετο κινδυνεύειν τὴν ψῆφον. ἔνοπλοι δὲ ἄνδρες παρῆσαν. ἔλεγεν ὅτι τοῦτο τῶν ἀρχόντων ἔργον εἴη, τοὺς τῇ ὀλιγαρχίᾳ ἐναντίους κολάζειν. οἱ δὲ βουλευταὶ ἐσκόπουν τί ποιήσειαν καὶ πῶς τῷ ἀνδρὶ βοηθήσειαν. τὸν μὲν λόγον ἤκουον, τὴν δὲ τῶν ὅπλων δύναμιν ἑώρων.

Ὁ οὖν Κριτίας τὸ τοῦ Θηραμένους ὄνομα ἐκ τοῦ καταλόγου ἐξήλειψεν. ἔπειτα ἔλεγεν ὅτι τοῖς Τριάκοντα ἐξείη τοῦτον ἀποκτείνειν. οὕτως ὁ ἄνθρωπος, ὃς πρότερον κρίσεως ἐτύγχανεν, ἐξαίφνης ἄνευ τῆς αὐτῆς φυλακῆς ἦν. ἡ γραφὴ μετεβλήθη, ἀλλὰ τὸ πρᾶγμα οὐ διὰ τοῦτο δικαιότερον ἐγένετο. τὴν γὰρ ἀσφάλειαν ὁ κατηγορῶν αὐτὸς ἀφῄρει.

Ὁ Θηραμένης πρὸς τὸν βωμὸν κατέφυγεν καὶ τοὺς θεοὺς καὶ τοὺς ἀνθρώπους ἐπεκαλεῖτο. ὁ δὲ Κριτίας τοῖς Ἕνδεκα παρέδωκεν αὐτόν. οἱ ὑπηρέται ἀπὸ τοῦ βωμοῦ ἀπέσπων, οἱ δὲ βουλευταὶ ἡσύχαζον φοβούμενοι. ὁ συγγραφεὺς τὴν ἀδικίαν οὐ νόμῳ γεγραμμένῳ μόνον δείκνυσιν, ἀλλὰ καὶ τοῖς σώμασι καὶ τῇ σιωπῇ τῶν παρόντων.

Ἐν τῇ ἡμετέρᾳ ἀσκήσει ἐρωτῶμεν τίς τὴν ψῆφον δοίη, τίς τὸν νόμον θείη, καὶ τίς τὸν φυλακῆς δεόμενον ἀφείη. ταῦτα οὐ νέαι μαρτυρίαι εἰσίν, ἀλλὰ τῆς διηγήσεως ἐξέτασις. ἡ γὰρ ὀρθὴ γραμματικὴ δεῖ καὶ τοὺς ποιοῦντας σαφεῖς ποιεῖν. μὴ τὸ «ἐκρίθη» λέγωμεν οὕτως, ὥστε κρύπτειν τίς ἔκρινεν καὶ τίς τὴν κρίσιν ἐκώλυσεν.

reading.translation:
After the Athenians’ defeat the Thirty ruled the city. Critias and Theramenes were among them. They did not agree about everything: Theramenes thought the government narrower than it should be, while Critias considered him an obstacle. The rulers sought more power, and the citizens feared that each might be the next to perish.

There was a list of three thousand citizens. Those on the list had to be judged by the council before execution, while the Thirty could kill those outside it. The list was therefore not merely a record of names: it made a difference to safety. Theramenes was among those on it and claimed judgment by the council.

Critias, seeing the council favorably disposed toward Theramenes, did not wish to risk the vote. Armed men were present. He said that it was the rulers’ duty to punish opponents of the oligarchy. The councilors considered what they should do and how they might help the man. They heard the argument, but saw the power of weapons.

Critias therefore erased Theramenes’ name from the list. He then said that the Thirty were permitted to kill him. Thus the man who previously enjoyed a right to judgment suddenly lacked the same protection. The record was changed, but the act did not thereby become more just. For the accuser himself was removing the protection.

Theramenes fled to the altar and called on gods and humans. Critias handed him over to the Eleven. The attendants dragged him from the altar, while the councilors remained quiet out of fear. The writer shows injustice not only through a written rule but also through the bodies and silence of those present.

In our exercise we ask who might give the vote, who might establish the rule, and who might release the person needing protection. These are not new testimonies but an examination of the narrative. For accurate grammar should also make the agents clear. Let us not say “he was judged” in a way that conceals who judged and who prevented judgment.

sections.title: 1. Present optatives of -μι verbs
body: The present optative retains the present stem: διδοίην, τιθείην, ἱσταίην, ἱείην. These forms are not aorists merely because they contain -ιη-. Learn them beside δίδωμι, τίθημι, ἵστημι, and ἵημι, and keep the reduplicated present stem visible.

Singular endings commonly follow -ίην, -ίης, -ίη; plural forms include διδοῖμεν/διδοίημεν and τιθεῖμεν/τιθείημεν. Compare ἱσταῖμεν and ἱεῖμεν. Context tells whether the verb means giving, placing, setting up, or sending. A potential statement adds ἄν; a subordinate oblique optative does not acquire it automatically.

sections.title: 2. Aorist optatives and voice
body: The aorist active forms lose the present reduplication: δοίην, θείην, σταίην, εἵην. With δίδωμι and τίθημι, compare plural δοῖμεν and θεῖμεν; with intransitive ἔστην, σταῖμεν. The aorist of ἵημι has the rough breathing in εἵην, and compounds such as ἀφείην are common.

Middle forms include δοίμην and θείμην, with third singular δοῖτο and θεῖτο. A form’s voice and lexical construction matter: θείη may mean “might establish,” while θεῖτο may mean “might adopt for himself.” Do not confuse the active optative θείη with passive ἐτέθη, or add the indicative aorist -κ- to δοίη.

sections.title: 3. Historical reporting and retained mood
body: In secondary sequence, an original finite indicative may appear as an optative: ἔλεγεν ὅτι τοῦτο δίκαιον εἴη. This reports what someone said, without turning the narrator into the original claimant. Original tense relations are preserved: a prior action is not made simultaneous merely because the main verb is past.

The original mood can be retained: ἔλεγεν ὅτι τοῦτο δίκαιόν ἐστιν. Mixed reporting is possible, so annotate each clause rather than enforcing a mechanical rule. An accusative-and-infinitive report remains an infinitive construction; it is not converted to an optative solely because φησί becomes ἔφη.

sections.title: 4. Indirect questions and reconstructing direct speech
body: After a historical verb of asking or considering, a direct indicative or deliberative subjunctive may become optative: τί δῶ; becomes ἠρώτα τί δοίη, “He asked what he should give.” A yes/no question still needs εἰ, “whether.” Keep the question’s focus, not just the verb ending.

Restore direct speech cautiously. A reported optative may reflect several original constructions, and pronouns depend on context. In ἠρώτα εἰ ὁ Κριτίας αὐτὸν ἀφείη, identify the person represented by αὐτόν before writing a direct question. The exercise may permit more than one defensible restoration; explain your choice.

sections.title: Meet Xenophon’s Hellenica
body: The selected episode takes us to the rule of the Thirty in 404–403 BCE. Critias and Theramenes belong to the ruling group, but their conflict exposes how quickly a legal protection can be removed. Read names, institutions, and the sequence of actions carefully. The narrative’s fear and silence matter alongside its explicit legal language.

The seven books cover Greek affairs from 411 to 362 BCE, beginning where Thucydides’ unfinished history breaks off. They follow Athens’ defeat in the Peloponnesian War, oligarchy and democratic restoration, Spartan ascendancy, shifting alliances, and the rise of Thebes. The closing battle at Mantinea leaves uncertainty rather than a simple declaration that one city has permanently won.

Xenophon organizes political and military events through commanders, assemblies, negotiations, speeches, and judgments about conduct. His attention is selective, and his experience and sympathies shape the narrative. Ask what a speech tries to accomplish, whose actions receive explanation, and what a compressed transition leaves unclear. A historian’s ordering of events can be as significant as an explicit verdict.

Reading invitation: start with Book 2, chapter 3, on the Thirty, then follow chapter 4 through resistance and restoration. Compare the settlement with the later Eleusis episode instead of stopping at the hopeful return to Athens. Our module’s question has grown from control of appetite to restraint in civic life: what practices let former enemies inhabit one city? Read the complete work as a sequence of difficult choices, not a storehouse of uncomplicated moral examples.
Distinguish membership in the governing group from agreement with every action its leaders take.

sections.title: Athens under the Thirty, 404–403 BCE
body: After Athens’ defeat in the Peloponnesian War, the Thirty imposed an oligarchic regime. Xenophon describes restrictions, killings, and conflict within the ruling group. Theramenes was himself an oligarch and a participant in this political world. Examining the injustice of his seizure does not require making him innocent of all earlier conduct.

The list of Three Thousand mattered because it distinguished those with a procedural protection from those whom the Thirty could kill on their own authority. A list that looks administrative can determine whose life receives a hearing.

sections.title: A protection removed by the accuser
body: Critias sees that the council may favor Theramenes and removes his name from the list. He then invokes the rule applicable to people outside it. The important sequence is protection, unilateral removal, and a claimed legal consequence. A change in paperwork does not make coercion disappear.

Theramenes appeals at the altar, but armed force and fear overcome the protection he seeks. The councilors’ silence is part of the scene. Do not assume silence means approval when the narrative also presents threats and weapons. The image reconstructs a council setting and deliberately avoids graphic violence.

sections.title: Identify each removed safeguard
body: Make a sequence of the protections lost: council judgment, inclusion on the list, and appeal at the altar. For each, name the person who acts and the people who could not or did not intervene. Rewrite “Theramenes was condemned” with enough active subjects to show the process.

Translate the historical reports and indirect questions, then restore one into possible direct speech. Explain any ambiguity rather than inventing a unique original wording. Finish with the final two paragraphs as a sustained translation and a sentence distinguishing a legal claim from a just procedure.
